title: Your Body's Defence Force, Part 1
summary: Your body is like a castle with walls, guards and alarm bells. Skin, tears and stomach acid keep most germs out, and hungry cells called phagocytes gobble up the ones that sneak in. A scientist discovered these germ-eating cells by poking thorns into see-through baby starfish!

sections.heading: The Castle Walls
paragraphs: Right now, as you read this sentence, you are under attack. Bacteria, viruses and fungal spores float in the air you breathe, sit on the book or screen you are touching, and ride along on the food you eat. Most of them are harmless, and many are even helpful. But some would happily move in and multiply if they could. The reason you are not sick all the time is your immune system, the body's defence network of cells, tissues and proteins that fights germs.

In the last few parts you watched scientists invent vaccines mostly by trial and error. In this part and the next, we look at the science they were missing: what is actually happening inside the body. A helpful way to picture it is a medieval castle. There are outer walls, there are guards who attack any intruder on sight, there are alarm bells, and, as you will see in Part 11, there are highly trained special forces who remember every enemy they have ever met.

The first line of defence is simply keeping germs out. Your biggest wall is your skin. The outer layer is made of flat, tough, dead cells stacked like roof tiles, packed with a protein called keratin, the same material as your fingernails. Most germs cannot get through unbroken skin. The skin is also fairly dry and slightly acidic, and its oils contain substances that slow the growth of many bacteria. Old skin cells are constantly flaking off, carrying germs away with them. That is why a cut or scrape matters: it is a hole in the castle wall.

Inside your nose, throat and lungs, the walls work differently. These surfaces are lined with mucus, a sticky liquid that traps dust and microbes like flypaper. In your airways, millions of tiny hair-like structures called cilia beat back and forth in waves, pushing the mucus upwards like a slow conveyor belt so it can be swallowed or coughed out. Sneezing and coughing are part of the same cleaning system, blasting unwanted particles back out of the body.

Your eyes are protected by tears, which wash them constantly each time you blink. Tears, saliva and the mucus in your nose contain an enzyme called lysozyme that can break down the walls of some bacteria. It was discovered in 1922 by Alexander Fleming, the same scientist who later found penicillin, reportedly after a drop of his own nasal mucus fell onto a dish of bacteria and dissolved some of them.

If germs are swallowed, they meet one of the harshest places in the body: the stomach. Stomach acid is strong enough to kill most microbes that arrive with food. Further along, the gut is home to trillions of friendly bacteria. Simply by living there and using up space and food, they make it harder for harmful bacteria to settle in. Even going to the toilet helps: the flow of urine flushes germs out of the urinary tract.

These barriers are not clever. They do not know one germ from another. But they stop the vast majority of invaders before any fighting begins. The question is what happens to the germs that do get through, through a splinter wound, a scraped knee or a breath of air carrying a virus. For a long time nobody knew. The answer began with a man staring through a microscope at a baby starfish.

sections.heading: A Thorn in Messina
paragraphs: Élie Metchnikoff, whose Russian name was Ilya Mechnikov, was born in 1845 in the village of Ivanovka, in what is now Ukraine. He was a zoologist, a scientist who studies animals, and he was especially interested in how simple sea creatures develop and digest their food. He was brilliant, restless and emotional, and he had already lived through hard times, including the death of his first wife from tuberculosis.

In 1882 he moved with his family to Messina, a port city on the island of Sicily in southern Italy, and set up a small private laboratory at home to study sea creatures. Among them were the larvae, or babies, of starfish. Starfish larvae are tiny and almost completely transparent, so under a microscope you can see right through them and watch individual cells moving about inside.

Metchnikoff noticed that some cells inside the larvae wandered freely, crawling about rather than staying put. He had seen cells like this swallowing bits of food in other simple animals, and one day, according to his own later account, a bold idea struck him: perhaps these wandering cells did not only digest food. Perhaps they also defended the animal against intruders.

To test it, he needed an intruder. He took a few small thorns from a plant in the garden next to his home and pushed them into some of the starfish larvae. Many retellings say they were rose thorns, but according to the usual accounts of his own story they were citrus thorns, from a little tangerine tree the family had decorated as a Christmas tree. He was so excited that he could hardly sleep that night. The next morning he looked again, and the thorns were surrounded by a crowd of the wandering cells, which had gathered around the invader as if trying to engulf it.

Metchnikoff realised that this was the same thing that happens when you get a splinter. The area around it becomes red and swollen, and pus forms. He suggested that pus is made largely of the body's own defender cells, which rush to the wound to attack the germs. He went on to watch cells swallow and digest bacteria in other animals too.

A professor named Carl Claus suggested a name for these cells: phagocytes, from Greek words meaning eating cells. The process of swallowing a germ is called phagocytosis. Metchnikoff argued that phagocytes are the body's front-line defence against infection.

Not everyone believed him. Many leading scientists thought immunity came from substances dissolved in the blood, such as the antitoxins Behring and Kitasato would describe in 1890. To them, phagocytes were just garbage collectors, cleaning up after the real battle. Metchnikoff spent years doing experiment after experiment to prove his case. In 1888 Louis Pasteur invited him to work at the new Pasteur Institute in Paris, where he stayed for the rest of his life. Waldemar Haffkine, the cholera vaccine pioneer from Part 9, had been one of his students back in Odessa. Today Metchnikoff is often called the father of innate immunity.

sections.heading: The Eaters: How Phagocytes Work
paragraphs: Phagocytes are a kind of white blood cell. Your blood looks red because it is crowded with red blood cells that carry oxygen, but mixed in among them are white blood cells, the body's mobile defenders. A healthy adult has roughly 4,000 to 11,000 white blood cells in every microlitre of blood, a drop smaller than a pinhead. Most of them are made in the bone marrow, the soft tissue inside your bones, and your body makes them in enormous numbers. Counting all types, a healthy adult makes roughly 100 billion new white blood cells every single day, many of them short-lived phagocytes that are constantly replaced.

The most common white blood cells are neutrophils, which make up about half to two thirds of the white cells in your blood. They are the castle's quick-reaction guards. When tissue is damaged or invaded, neutrophils can begin arriving within minutes. Each one is about 10 micrometres across, roughly a seventh of the width of a human hair. They do not live long, usually only a day or a few days, which is one reason the body has to keep making so many.

How does a neutrophil find a germ? It follows a trail of chemicals. Bacteria release certain molecules, and damaged cells and other immune cells release signals too. Phagocytes can sense which direction these chemicals are coming from and crawl towards the strongest smell, a bit like a shark following a trace of blood in the water. This is called chemotaxis. To leave the bloodstream, neutrophils grab onto the walls of tiny blood vessels near the trouble, roll along them, and squeeze out between the cells of the vessel wall into the tissue.

When a phagocyte reaches a bacterium, it grabs it with receptors on its surface, molecules that work a little like hands. Then the cell stretches its outer edge around the bacterium until the germ is completely enclosed in a bubble inside the cell. That bubble merges with other bubbles full of digestive chemicals, and the germ is broken apart. A neutrophil takes about nine minutes on average to swallow a bacterium.

Phagocytes also use chemical weapons. When a neutrophil swallows something, it suddenly uses much more oxygen and turns some of it into highly reactive molecules that damage microbes. One enzyme in neutrophils even makes hypochlorous acid, a chemical closely related to the active ingredient in household bleach. In some situations neutrophils can also throw out sticky, web-like nets made of their own DNA, which trap and kill bacteria outside the cell. When an infected wound fills with pus, much of that pus is made of neutrophils that have done their job and died.

Neutrophils have bigger, slower partners. Monocytes travel in the blood and, when they move into tissues, grow into macrophages, a word meaning big eaters. Macrophages are about twice as wide as neutrophils, live much longer, and stay on patrol in places like the lungs, liver and skin. They eat germs, old and worn-out cells and debris. Another type, called dendritic cells, after their long finger-like branches, swallow germs too, but their most important job is to carry pieces of those germs to the adaptive immune system, the special forces you will meet in the next part. They are the messengers between the two halves of your defence force.

sections.heading: Alarm Bells: Inflammation and Fever
paragraphs: Think about what happens when you get a splinter in your finger. Within hours the skin around it may turn red, feel warm, swell up and hurt. That is inflammation, and although it is uncomfortable, it is a sign that your defence force has sounded the alarm.

The alarm starts with guard cells already sitting in the tissue, such as macrophages and mast cells. They carry special sensors, called pattern recognition receptors, that can detect molecules found on many kinds of germs but not on our own cells, such as pieces of bacterial cell walls. These sensors do not identify an exact germ. They simply recognise that something germ-like is there. One important family of these sensors, called Toll-like receptors, was first discovered in fruit flies, and work on how they help start immune responses was honoured with the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2011.

Once the alarm is raised, the guard cells release chemical messages. Mast cells, for example, release histamine, which makes nearby blood vessels wider and leakier. More blood flows to the area, which is why it looks red and feels warm. Fluid leaks out of the vessels into the tissue, which causes swelling. The leakiness also lets white blood cells and helpful proteins from the blood pour into the battle zone. The pain is partly caused by chemicals that sensitise nerves, and it encourages you to protect the injured spot while it heals.

Some of the helpful proteins that arrive belong to a group called the complement system. These are dozens of different proteins that float in the blood in an inactive state. When they meet a germ, they set off a chain reaction, each protein switching on the next like a row of falling dominoes. The end result can coat the germ so phagocytes grab it more easily, call in more white blood cells, or even punch holes in the outer surface of some bacteria so they burst.

There are other innate defenders too. Natural killer cells, a type of white blood cell, patrol the body looking for our own cells that have become infected by viruses or have turned cancerous. Infected cells often look a bit wrong on the outside, and natural killer cells can recognise that and order those cells to self-destruct, sacrificing them before the virus inside can spread further. Infected cells can also release warning molecules called interferons, which tell neighbouring cells to raise their defences against viruses.

Sometimes the alarm spreads to the whole body, and you get a fever. Your body temperature is controlled by a small region at the base of the brain called the hypothalamus, which works like a thermostat. During an infection, immune cells release messenger molecules that travel to the brain and turn the thermostat up. The body then acts as though it is too cold. Blood vessels in the skin narrow to keep heat in, and muscles start shivering to make heat, which is why people with a rising fever often feel chilly even though their temperature is going up.

Scientists think fever evolved because it can help. Many germs grow best at normal body temperature, and a higher temperature can slow some of them down. Warmth also seems to make some immune cells work faster. Evidence for this comes even from animals that cannot make their own heat: some grasshoppers move to warmer places when infected by a fungus, raising their body temperature by a few degrees, and honeybee colonies can warm their hive in response to a fungal infection of their young. Fever still makes people feel unwell, and how to manage it is something for doctors and trusted adults, not a science book.

sections.heading: Paul Ehrlich and the Side Chains
paragraphs: While Metchnikoff was championing cells, many other scientists, especially in Germany, believed the most important defence was something dissolved in the blood. The discovery of antitoxins in 1890 seemed to prove their point. Historians sometimes call this the argument between the cellular school (cells do the fighting) and the humoral school, from an old word for body fluids (substances in the blood do the fighting). The leading thinker on the blood side was Paul Ehrlich.

Ehrlich was born in 1854 in Strehlen, in the Prussian province of Silesia (today Strzelin in Poland). As a student he became fascinated by dyes. The German chemical industry was producing bright new artificial dyes, and Ehrlich discovered that different dyes stuck to different parts of cells. Using them, he could tell apart types of white blood cells that looked identical without stain. While still a student, he discovered mast cells, the histamine-releasing alarm cells you met above.

As you saw in Part 9, Ehrlich helped make diphtheria antitoxin practical by working out how to measure its strength. Thinking about how antitoxin could find and grab a toxin, he came up with a bold idea, published in detail in 1897, called the side-chain theory. He imagined that cells carry many different molecular side chains on their surface, each shaped to grab a particular substance, rather like keys sticking out of a lock. When a toxin attached to its matching side chain, the cell would respond by making many extra copies of that side chain and releasing the surplus into the blood. Those free-floating side chains would be the antitoxins, ready to catch more toxin before it reached the cells.

Not all of the details turned out to be right, but the central idea was remarkably close to the truth. Antibodies really do have specific shapes that fit specific targets, and they really are made by cells and released into the blood. Ehrlich also helped popularise the German word Antikörper, which became antibody in English, in his writings in the early 1890s.

Ehrlich dreamed of what he called a magic bullet, a chemical that would hit only a germ and leave the body unharmed, just as an antibody hits only its own target. In 1909, he and his Japanese colleague Sahachiro Hata found a compound, number 606 in their long list of tested chemicals, that could kill the bacterium that causes syphilis. Sold as Salvarsan from 1910, it was one of the first modern drugs designed to target a germ.

So who won the argument, the cells or the blood? In 1908 the Nobel committee gave its answer: both. The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was shared by Metchnikoff and Ehrlich, in recognition of their work on immunity. Around the same time, the British scientist Almroth Wright, the typhoid vaccine pioneer from Part 9, showed that substances in the blood, which he called opsonins, coat bacteria and make them much easier for phagocytes to swallow. The two kinds of defence were not rivals at all. They were teammates.

sections.heading: Name Tags and Y-Shaped Keys
paragraphs: To understand vaccines, two words matter more than almost any others: antigen and antibody.

An antigen is any molecule that the immune system can recognise. Very often it is a protein or sugar on the outside of a germ, such as a spike on the surface of a virus or a molecule in a bacterium's outer coat. Toxins, like the diphtheria toxin from Part 9, can be antigens too. You can think of antigens as name tags. Each kind of germ wears its own particular set of name tags, and the immune system learns to read them. The word antigen was originally short for antibody generator, because antigens are what cause antibodies to be made. A germ's name tag is often large, and an antibody actually grips just one small patch of it, called an epitope.

An antibody is a protein made by the immune system that locks onto one specific antigen. Antibodies are shaped like the letter Y. Each one is built from four protein chains: two longer ones called heavy chains and two shorter ones called light chains, joined together by chemical bonds. An antibody is incredibly small, only about 10 nanometres across, which is roughly ten thousand times thinner than a human hair.

The two arms of the Y are where the magic happens. The tip of each arm has a shape that fits one particular antigen, a bit like a key that fits only one lock, or a glove that fits only one hand. Because both arms are the same, one antibody can grab two copies of its antigen at once. The stem of the Y does a different job: it acts like a handle that other parts of the immune system, such as phagocytes and complement proteins, can recognise and grab.

Once antibodies lock on, they protect the body in several ways. They can neutralise a germ or toxin by covering the parts it needs to attack cells, just as Behring's antitoxin did. They can clump germs together, since each antibody has two arms, making them easier to clean up. They can coat a germ like a label saying eat me, so phagocytes swallow it faster, which is exactly what Almroth Wright's opsonins were. And they can switch on the complement system to punch holes in bacteria.

Humans make five main classes of antibody, each with its own speciality. IgG is the most common in the blood and gives most long-term protection; it is also the only class that can cross from a mother to her unborn baby, giving newborns borrowed protection for their first months. IgA guards the wet surfaces of the body and is found in tears, saliva and breast milk. IgM is usually the first type made when the body meets a new germ. IgE is involved in allergies, and IgD helps certain immune cells sense their targets. The letters Ig stand for immunoglobulin, the scientific name for antibodies.

Perhaps the most astonishing fact is how many different antibodies the body can make. Estimates suggest a person can produce on the order of billions of different antibody shapes, enough to match almost any antigen, including germs that have never existed before. Working out the detailed structure of antibodies earned Rodney Porter and Gerald Edelman the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1972. But which cells make all those antibodies, and how does the body pick the right one? That belongs to the special forces of the next part.

sections.heading: Why the Fast Team Is Not Always Enough
paragraphs: Everything in this part, the barriers, phagocytes, inflammation, complement, natural killer cells and fever, belongs to what scientists call innate immunity. Innate means something you are born with. It is fast: it starts working within minutes to hours of an infection. It is also general: it recognises broad patterns that many germs share, so it can respond to almost anything. Some form of innate immunity is found in nearly all living things, from insects to plants, which use their own chemical alarm signals to fight off disease.

Most of the time, innate immunity wins. The vast majority of germs that get past your barriers are cleaned up by phagocytes and complement before you ever notice. But innate immunity has some important weaknesses.

First, it does not learn. The tenth time a neutrophil meets a particular type of bacterium, it responds in roughly the same way as the first time. It has no memory of past battles, so it cannot get better at fighting a particular enemy.

Second, some germs have evolved tricks to dodge it. Some bacteria grow thick, slippery outer coats called capsules that phagocytes find hard to grip. Some can survive inside phagocytes after being swallowed; the bacterium that causes tuberculosis, for example, can live for a long time inside macrophages. Viruses hide inside our own cells, where phagocytes cannot see them, and some viruses can switch off the warning signals that infected cells send out.

Third, some germs are simply too fast or too dangerous. A germ that multiplies extremely quickly, or that releases a powerful toxin, can cause serious harm before the general defences get it under control. The diphtheria toxin from Part 9 is a good example: phagocytes cannot stop a poison that is already spreading through the blood. What stops it is an antibody shaped to fit that one toxin exactly.

And that is the key. The antitoxins, the protection that survivors of smallpox had, and the immunity that vaccines produce are not mainly the work of the fast, general guards. They are specific: protection against one particular germ or toxin. They improve with experience. And they can last for years, sometimes a lifetime. That points to a second, slower, smarter part of the immune system, one with the ability to remember.

In the next part we meet these special forces: the B cells that make antibodies, the T cells that coordinate the defence and destroy infected cells, and the memory cells that explain why surviving a disease, or receiving a vaccine, can protect you for years. It is the part of the story that finally explains what Lady Mary, Onesimus, Jenner and Pasteur had all been relying on without knowing it.

deepDive: The cellular-versus-humoral debate of the 1880s to 1900s is a classic case of a scientific argument in which both sides were partly right. Metchnikoff's phagocytes are central to innate immunity, while the antitoxins of Behring, Kitasato and Ehrlich turned out to be antibodies, products of the adaptive system. The two systems are tightly linked: antibodies and complement act as opsonins that make phagocytosis far more efficient, and dendritic cells and macrophages present antigens that switch on adaptive responses. For decades innate immunity was treated as a crude first line of defence. That changed in the 1990s. In 1989 the immunologist Charles Janeway proposed that innate cells must carry receptors for conserved microbial patterns, and that these receptors also help switch on adaptive immunity. In 1996 Jules Hoffmann's group showed that fruit flies lacking a gene called Toll could not fight fungal infections, and in 1998 Bruce Beutler identified a related receptor in mice (TLR4) that detects lipopolysaccharide, a component of the outer membrane of many bacteria. Beutler and Hoffmann shared the 2011 Nobel Prize with Ralph Steinman, who discovered dendritic cells in 1973. Humans have about ten Toll-like receptors, each sensing a different class of microbial molecule, such as bacterial cell-wall pieces, flagellin, or viral genetic material. This matters for vaccines. Many vaccine adjuvants work, at least in part, by stimulating innate sensors, and modern mRNA vaccines use chemically modified building blocks partly to avoid triggering excessive innate inflammation, as Part 18 explains. Numbers in immunology are often given only roughly because they vary between people and over time. Neutrophils alone are produced at about 100 billion per day in a healthy adult, and a typical microlitre of blood contains about 4,000 to 11,000 white cells. Estimates of the number of distinct antibodies a person can make range from billions upwards, depending on how they are counted. There is also active research on whether innate immunity has a kind of short-term memory, sometimes called trained immunity, in which an earlier challenge (BCG vaccination is a much-studied example) changes how innate cells respond to later, unrelated infections. This is an area of ongoing study rather than settled fact.
